title: Hypothermia indoors: living in a cold house
summary: Weeks in a cold house bring on hypothermia slowly, mostly in older people and babies, often with little shivering. The indoor temperatures health bodies give, the signs to check for, who to check on, and how to rewarm someone gently when no help is coming.

steps.text: Put a thermometer where people sit and where they sleep. Aim for at least 18 °C (64 °F) in rooms people spend a lot of time in (UKHSA keep warm, Janssen 2023).
steps.warn: Older and sick people may need it warmer, and many of them do not feel the cold (PHE 2014, Janssen 2023).

steps.text: Know who is at risk: people over 65, babies under 1, people with heart or lung disease or diabetes, anyone on medicines, drink or drugs, and anyone living alone (Health Canada cold, MMWR 2006, MMWR 2015).
Check on them often, in person (CDC winter). Early hypothermia looks like ordinary confusion or tiredness (MMWR chronic).

Look for the signs: in adults, cold pale skin, slurred speech, fumbling, confusion and drowsiness, with or without shivering. In babies, cold or bright red cold skin, floppiness and very low energy (CDC hypothermia, NHS hypothermia).
steps.warn: Headache, drowsiness and confusion near anything burning can be carbon monoxide. Get everyone into fresh air first.

steps.text: Rewarm gently: warmest room, damp clothes off, dry layers with the head covered and insulation underneath. Warm sweet drinks only if fully awake (NHS hypothermia, WMS-Hypo).
steps.warn: No hot bath, no rubbing arms or legs, no alcohol (NHS hypothermia).

steps.text: If they are confused or not shivering, keep them lying down and put heat on the chest, armpits and back: an electric blanket, skin-to-skin, or wrapped warm bottles. For a baby, use skin-to-skin with a warm adult, and no bottle or electric blanket (Lullaby winter, Tasmania Fire bedrooms). Check the skin every 20 to 30 minutes (CDC hypothermia, WMS-Hypo).
steps.warn: NHS says no hot-water bottle; rescue guidelines allow wrapped warm bottles on the trunk. Cold skin burns easily, even from lukewarm bottles on bare skin (WMS-Hypo, NHS hypothermia).

steps.text: Not breathing: check for a full minute, then start CPR and keep warming. See First aid.
If a room has gone below freezing, check fingers, toes, ears and nose for frostbite. Thaw only where it cannot freeze again (CCOHS cold health).

notes:
## Why it creeps up indoors

Hypothermia means the body's core has dropped below 35 °C (95 °F). That is an emergency (NHS hypothermia, CDC hypothermia). Outdoors it comes fast. Indoors it comes slowly, over days in a cold house, and people often don't notice it happening.

- CDC describes "chronic" hypothermia in people exposed to indoor cold below about 16 °C (60 °F) for a long time, mostly people who feel the cold poorly, move little and eat poorly (MMWR chronic).
- In US data, 23% of people with hypothermia were at home when it began, and in an Alabama study almost half the hypothermia deaths happened indoors (MMWR 2006).
- In a Wisconsin review of hypothermia deaths, about half the people lived alone, and some of those found indoors had a furnace that was off or broken (MMWR 2015).
- Older people make less heat, control their temperature less well and sense cold less well (PHE 2014, MMWR 2015). Many shiver less or not at all, so shivering is not a reliable warning (Pharmacy Times). Some illnesses and many medicines also blunt shivering (WMS-Hypo).
- Babies under 1 lose heat faster than adults and can't make enough heat by shivering (Simcoe Muskoka).
- The first signs are vague changes in thinking and judgement, easily taken for something else (MMWR chronic).

## Who is most at risk

- People over 65, and babies under 1 year (Health Canada cold, CCOHS cold health).
- People with heart or lung disease, diabetes, poor balance or other long-term illness (MMWR 2006, PHE 2014).
- People on some medicines, including some cold remedies, or who drink or use drugs (CDC hypothermia, Pharmacy Times).
- Anyone living alone (MMWR 2015, NHS hypothermia).
- Anyone in a poorly insulated home with no heat or no power (Health Canada cold).

## How cold is too cold

| Figure | Who says it | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| 18 °C (64 °F) | WHO Housing and Health Guidelines, 2018, as reported in two reviews | Minimum for the general population in cold seasons. A higher minimum may be needed for older people, children and people with long-term illness (Janssen 2023, Barlow 2023) |
| At least 18 °C (64 °F) | UK Health Security Agency, 2026 | For rooms you spend a lot of time in, such as the living room or bedroom (UKHSA keep warm) |
| 18 °C day; may drop at night | Public Health England review, 2014 | Below 18 °C, blood pressure and clotting risk start to rise. Keeping 18 °C overnight may help people over 65 or with illness; healthy people with enough bedding can go cooler at night (PHE 2014) |
| 16 to 20 °C (61 to 68 °F) | The Lullaby Trust (UK) | A room where a baby sleeps (Lullaby room) |
| Comfortable for you | Public Health Agency of Canada | A room where a baby sleeps; overheating is a risk factor for SIDS (PHAC baby sleep) |
| Below 16 °C (60 °F) for long periods | CDC | Where chronic hypothermia occurs in people at risk (MMWR chronic) |
| Thermostat above 15.6 °C (60 °F) | CDC | Suggested public advice after a review of hypothermia deaths (MMWR 2006) |
| 12 °C (55 °F) | Manitoba Health | Lowest thermostat setting to stop pipes freezing. A pipe figure, not a health one (Manitoba cold) |

The UK used to advise 21 °C (70 °F) for living rooms and 18 °C for bedrooms; the 2014 review replaced that with a single 18 °C (PHE 2014).

These are targets for normal times, and the evidence behind any exact number is thin. The review that set 18 °C called its evidence very limited, and a 2023 review found too little to fix thresholds for different groups (PHE 2014, Janssen 2023). Treat 18 °C as a sign to act, not a line where safety ends.

In an outage you may not reach these figures. Then heat one room and the bed, not the house, and check people more: see [Stay warm in one heated room](#guides/skill_staying_warm). Put a thermometer where people sit and where they sleep. CDC asks people over 65 to check the temperature in their home often in very cold weather (CDC winter).

## Signs to check for

**Adults:** shivering (may be weak or missing in older people), cold pale skin, a puffy face, slurred or slow speech, fumbling hands, memory loss, confusion and drowsiness (CDC hypothermia, NHS hypothermia, Pharmacy Times). Severe: shivering stops, breathing slows, the person stops responding (CCOHS cold health).

**Babies:** cold to the touch, bright red cold skin, floppy, very low energy, unusually quiet and sleepy, not feeding (CDC hypothermia, NHS hypothermia, Manitoba cold). A baby under 1 should never sleep in a cold room (CDC winter).

A baby's hands and feet are normally cool. Feel the chest or the back of the neck instead. Sweaty or clammy means too hot, which is also dangerous (Lullaby winter). Babies don't need hats indoors, and hot-water bottles don't belong in any baby's sleep space (Lullaby winter, PHAC baby sleep). If you think a baby is cold, add a layer of clothing, or dress the baby in sleepwear suited to the room (Lullaby winter, PHAC baby sleep). Health Canada advises no loose blankets in a baby's sleep space, and a baby sleeps alone in its own crib, cradle or bassinet (Health Canada safe sleep).

**Could it be carbon monoxide?** Headache, drowsiness and confusion in a room where something is burning can be CO. Get everyone into fresh air first and think second: see [Carbon monoxide](#browse/hazards/co_gas).

## Checking on people

- Check on older friends and neighbours often, and make sure their homes are heated properly (CDC winter). Plan regular checks on older or vulnerable relatives and neighbours, and make sure they have food, clothing and heat (Manitoba cold).
- Visit, phone, bring warm clothing and a safe way to keep warm, or take them somewhere warm (Simcoe Muskoka). If a home can't be kept warm, arrange for them to stay elsewhere if you can (Simcoe Muskoka). The simplest fix is often to bring them into your warm room.
- CDC suggests checking that older people have heat, medicines and supplies (MMWR 2006).
- The sources say "often" (CDC winter) and "regularly" (Manitoba cold). About half the people in the Wisconsin review of hypothermia deaths lived alone (MMWR 2015), so anyone living alone needs someone who looks in on them in person.

On each check, look at: the thermometer, whether they are eating hot food and drinking, whether their bedding and clothes are dry, how they talk and move, and whether any heater is safe and the CO alarm works.

## Rewarming someone gently

**Shivering and making sense** (cold, not yet badly hypothermic):
- Into the warmest room, out of damp clothes, into dry layers or a sleeping bag with the head covered, with insulation underneath (NHS hypothermia, WMS-Hypo).
- Warm sweet drinks and food if they are fully awake and can swallow. Warm, not hot enough to scald (WMS-Hypo, NHS hypothermia).
- Let shivering do the work while they are wrapped. Keep them resting about 30 minutes before they get up and move about (WMS-Hypo).

**Confused, drowsy or not shivering:**
- Keep them lying down and handle them gently (WMS-Hypo, Health Canada cold).
- Warm the chest, neck, head and groin, or the armpits, chest and back, not the arms and legs (CDC hypothermia, WMS-Hypo). An electric blanket over the chest works (CDC hypothermia). So does skin-to-skin contact under loose dry blankets (CDC hypothermia). For a baby, use skin-to-skin only, with no bottle or electric blanket (Lullaby winter, Tasmania Fire bedrooms).
- No hot bath, no heat lamp, no rubbing the arms or legs, no alcohol (NHS hypothermia).
- NHS advice is not to use a hot-water bottle. Rescue guidelines do use warm bottles on the trunk, wrapped, and checked every 20 to 30 minutes for reddening, because cold skin burns easily: burns have come from bottles of lukewarm water on bare hypothermic skin (NHS hypothermia, WMS-Hypo). If you use one, wrap it, keep it warm not hot, and look.
- Not breathing: check breathing for a full minute, then CPR. People this cold can look dead and not be (WMS-Hypo). See [First aid, cold and heat](#ref/reference_first_aid/cold_and_heat).

## Frostbite indoors

Frostbite happens when tissue falls below 0 °C (32 °F). Toes, fingers, ears and nose go first, and older adults and babies are more at risk (CCOHS cold health). An unheated house in a Canadian winter can go below freezing inside: one case in a CDC report on hypothermia deaths was in a bus where it was −26 °C (−15 °F) inside (MMWR 2006).

- Frostnip: skin yellowish or white but still soft (Health Canada cold).
- Frostbite: numbness, waxy or firm skin; later white, grey or blistered fingers, toes, ear lobes or nose tip (CDC hypothermia, Manitoba cold).
- Rewarm in water just above body temperature (Health Canada cold); see [Cold](#browse/hazards/cold) for the 37 to 39 °C soak. Don't rub it, and don't warm it at a fireplace, heating pad or electric blanket (CDC hypothermia).
- Don't thaw it if it may freeze again (CCOHS cold health).
